elements.text: Full Paper: A new bis(etheranhydride), 1,1-bis[4-(3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl] cyclododecane dianhydride (BDPCD), was prepared in three steps starting from nitrodisplacement of 4-nitrophthalonitrile with 2,2-bis(4-hydroxyphenyl) cyclododecane (BHPC), followed by alkaline hydrolysis of the intermediate bis(ether dinitrile) (BCPPC) and subsequent dehydration of the resulting bis(ether diacid) (BAPPC). A series of new highly soluble poly(ether imide)s having tertbutyl substituents, together with noncoplanar and pendent cardo groups were prepared from such bis(ether anhydride) (BDPCD) with various diamines by a conventional two-stage synthesis including the polyaddition and chemical cyclodehydration. The resulting poly(ether imide)s had inherent viscosities in the range of 0.50–0.86 dL  g<sup>-1</sup>. The GPC measurement revealed that the polymers exhibited number-average and weight-average molecular weight up to 63 000 and 115 000, respectively. All the polymers showed typical amorphous diffraction patterns. All of the poly(ether imide)s showed excellent solubility and were readily dissolved in various solvents such asN-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP),N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), pyridine, cyclohexanone and tetrahydrofuran. Most of the polymers could be dissolved in chloroform as high as 30 wt.-% concentration. These polymers had glass transition temperatures $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$in the range of $2 3 0 { - } 2 6 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$. Thermogravimetric analysis(TGA) showed thatall polymers werestable,with10% weights loss recorded above $4 3 4 ^ { \circ } \dot { \mathrm { C } }$and $4 0 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$in nitrogen and air, respectively. These transparent, tough and flexible polymer films could be obtained by solution casting from the DMAc solution. These polymer films had tensile strengths in the range of80–102 MPaand tensilemoduliinthe rangeof1.7–2.0 GPa.
Highly Organosoluble Polyimides with Pendent Cyclododecane Group: Synthesis and Characterization
Der-Jang Liaw,\* I-Wen Chen, Ming-Che Yang
Department of Chemical Engineering, National Taiwan University of Science and Technology, Taipei, Taiwan Fax: 886-2-23781441 or 886-2-27376644; E-mail: liaw@ch.ntust.edu.tw, liaw8484@yahoo.com.tw
Keywords: 1,1-Bis[4-(3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane dianhydride (BDPCD); bulky pendent; polyimides
Introduction

Aromatic polyimides are well accepted as thermally stable materials.<sup>[1]</sup> Recently, significant synthetic effort has been centered on improving thermal and mechanical properties and solubility through the synthesis of new diamine or dianhydride monomer. The incorporation of bulky pendant groups<sup>[2]</sup> into rigid polymer backbones has led to the most success.

Introduction of pendent loops along the polymer back bone has been shown to impart greater solubility as well as better mechanical and thermal properties to the resulting ‘‘cardo’’ polymer, which is of particular importance in aromatic heterocyclic polymers with rigid chains.<sup>[3]</sup> Also, it has been reported that the presence of cardo groups such as fluorene, phthalide, phthalimidine, anthrone in the repeat unit of polyimide similarly results in enhanced solubility as well as high thermal properties of polymer.<sup>[3–6]</sup>

Recently, several studies have also made focus on the adoption polyalicyl dianhydrides<sup>[7–9]</sup> or diamines containing alicyclic structures<sup>[10,11]</sup> for the preparation of polyimides that were thermally stable and easier to process. In our previous studies, we synthesized new cardo polyimides with bulky pendent alicyclic cyclododecylidene groups and polyimide with hydroxyl group.<sup>[12–17]</sup> The obtained polymers showed good thermal stability and enhanced solubility.

According to these research trends, the present investigation deals with the synthesis of a new class of polyimides which will be derived from new bis(ether anhydride), 1,1- bis[4-(3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl] cyclododecane dianhydride (BDPCD). The properties of these polymers such as solubility, crystallinity, as well as thermal and tensile properties are also being investigated herein.
Experimental Part
Materials

Cyclododecanone (from ACROS), butylmercaptan, 4-nitrophthalonitrile (from ACROS), anhydrous potassium carbonate, hydrazine monohydrate (ACROS), and acetic anhydride (from Merck) were used as received. N,N-Dimethylacetamide (DMAc) and N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) and pyridine were purified by distillation under reduced pressure over calcium hydride before use. 4,4<sup>0</sup>-methylenedianiline (DA-2) and 4,4<sup>0</sup>-oxydianiline (DA-4) were purified by sublimation under vacuum from Wakayama Seika Co. In addition, the following compounds, 2,2<sup>0</sup>-dimethyl-4,4<sup>0</sup>-bis(4-aminophenoxy)biphenyl (DA-1, m.p. 138–139 8C),<sup>[15–18]</sup> 1,4-bis(4-aminophenoxy)-2-tert-butylbenzene (DA-3, m.p. 134–135 8C),<sup>[16–18]</sup> 2,2-bis[4-(4-aminophenoxy)phenyl]norbornane (DA-5, m.p. 149–150 8C),<sup>[16–18]</sup> 1,1-bis[4-(4-aminophenoxy)phenyl]- 4-tert-butylcyclohexane (DA-6, m.p. 171–172 8C),<sup>[16–18]</sup> and 2,2-bis[4-(4-aminophenoxy)phenyl]adamantane, (DA-7, m.p. $2 4 1 - 2 \bar { 4 } 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ) ^ { [ 1 6 - 1 8 ] }$were synthesized and purified by our laboratory according to the methods previously reported.
Monomers Synthesis

Scheme 1 illustrates the synthesis of 1,1-bis[4-hydroxyphenyl]cyclododecane (BHPC), 1,1-bis[4-(3,4-dicyanophenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane (BCPPC), 1,1-bis[4-(3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane (BAPPC), and 1,1- bis[4-(3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane dianhydride (BDPCD).
1,1-Bis[4-hydroxyphenyl]cyclododecane (BHPC)<sup>[19]</sup>

A flask was charged with a mixture of cyclododecanone (4.7 g, 26 mmol), phenol (16.4 g, 60 mmol), and butylmercaptan (0.15 mL). Heat was applied and when the reaction mixture became liquid at $5 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$, anhydrous hydrogen chloride was introduced until the solution became saturated. Stirring was continued at $6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for several hours, during which period white solids began to separate out from the reddish-orange reaction mixture. The solid obtained was filtered off, washed with dichloromethane, and dried to afford BHPC in 83% yield. It was recrystallized from toluene, m.p. 207–209 8C. The IR spectrum (KBr) exhibited absorptions at 3 200–3 300 cm<sup>-1</sup> (O–H).
1,1-Bis[4-(3,4-dicyanophenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane (BCPPC)

In a 100-mL round-bottomed flask, 3 g (8.5 mmol) of cyclododecanone and 3.65 g (21.08 mmol) of 4-nitrophthalonitrile were dissolved in 20 mL of dry DMF. Anhydrous potassium carbonate 4.35 g (21.95 mmol) was added and the suspension was stirred at room temperature for two days. The reaction mixture was then poured into 500 mL of water to give a pale-yellow solid product which was washed repeatedly with water and methanol, filtered out, and dried. The crude product was then recrystallized twice from acetonitrile to obtain white crystal of bis(ether dinitrile) (BCPPC) in 73% yield; m.p. 211–212 8C.
IR (KBr): 2 224 (C:N) and 1 247 cm<sup>-1</sup> (C–O).
1,1-Bis[4-(3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane (BAPPC)

In a 100-mL round-bottomed flask, 3 g (4.96 mmol) of bis(ether dinitrile) (BCPPC) was suspended in a solution of 5.95 g (0.11 mol) potassium hydroxide in 75 mL/75 mL of water-ethanol, in which the solid bis(ether dinitrile) had been dissolved within 2 h. Hydrogen peroxide (10 mL) was added dropwise over a period of 0.5 h to the suspension solution.

Reflux was continued for three days until the evolution of ammonia had ceased. After filtration, the cooled filtrate was diluted with 200 mL of water and acidified by concentrated HCl. The precipitated bis(ether diacid) (BAPPC) was filtered off and washed thoroughly with distillated water until the filtrate was neutral. The yield was 80%; m.p. 152– 153 8C.
IR (KBr): 2 500–3 600 (C(O)O–H), 1 706 (C O), and $1 2 2 8 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } ( \mathrm { C } - 0 - \mathrm { C } ) .$
1,1-Bis[4-(3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane Dianhydride (BDPCD)

In a 100-mL round-bottomed flask, 1.0 g (1.47 mmol) of bis(ether diacid) BAPPC) was suspended in 3 mL of glacial acetic acid and 3 mL of acetic anhydride. The mixture was boiled under reflux for 24 h. Then, the mixture was filtered and left to crystallize overnight. The precipitated product was filtered out and further recrystallized from acetic anhydride. The brown crystal obtained was filtered out, washed with dry hexane, and dried at $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for 12 h under vacuum to give bis(ether anhydride) (BDPCD).The yield was 60%, m. p. 212– 213 8C.
Polymerization Procedures

To a stirred solution ofDA-1 0.3084 g (0.78 mmol) in 4 mL of DMAc, bis(ether anhydride) (BDPCD) 0.5008 g (0.78 mmol) was gradually added. The mixture was stirred at room temperature for 2 h under argon atmosphere to form the poly(ether amic acid) precursor. Chemical imidization was carried out by adding extra 3 mL of DMAc, 1 mL of acetic anhydride, and 1 mL pyridine into the above-mentioned poly(ether amic acid) solution with stirring at room temperature for 1 h, and then heating to $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for 3 h. The homogeneous solution was subsequently poured into methanol and the white stringy precipitate was filtered off, washed with methanol and hot water, and then dried at 100 8C for 24 h to afford poly(ether imide) PI-1. The inherent viscosity of the polymer in N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc) was 0.50 dL $\cdot \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$measured at a concentration of 0.5 g  dL<sup>-1</sup> at $3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$

Measurements

The inherent viscosities of all polymers were measured in DMAc using an Ubbelohde viscometer. Elemental analysis was performed on a Perkin-Elmer 2400 instrument. NMR spectra were obtained using a JEOL EX-400 operating at 399.65 MHz for proton and 100.40 MHz for carbon. Weight-average $( \bar { M } _ { \mathrm { w } } )$and number-average $( \overline { { M } } _ { \mathrm { w } } )$molecular weight were determined by gel permeation chromatography (GPC). Four Waters (Ultrastyragel) columns $3 0 0 \times 7 . 7$mm (guard, 10<sup>5</sup>, 10<sup>4</sup>, 10<sup>3</sup>, 500 A<sup>˚</sup> in a series) were used for GPC analysis with tetrahydrofuran (THF) (1 mL $\cdot \operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 } )$as the eluent. The eluents were monitored with a UV detector (Gilson model 116) at 254 nm. Polystyrene was used as the standard. Wide-angle X-ray diffraction patterns were performed at room temperature with film specimens on a X-ray diffractometer (Philips model PW 1710) using Ni filtered $\mathrm { { C u - K } } _ { \alpha }$radiation (30 kV, 25 mA). Samples for thermogravimetric analysis (ULVAC, model 7000) were heated under nitrogen or air $( 6 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } \cdot \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 } )$) at a heating rate of $2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } \cdot \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis was performed on a Du Pont 2000 differential scanning calorimeter. Glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$was taken at the inflection point. Mechanical properties were determined from stress-strain curves obtained with an Orientec Tensilon with a load cell of 10 kg. A gauge of 3 cm and a strain rate of $2 \mathrm { c m } \cdot \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$were used for this study. Measurements were performed at room temperature with five film specimens (0.5 cm wide, 6 cm long, and ca. 0.05 mm thick). Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) was performed on a Perkin Elmer DMA 7e system at a heating rate of $5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } \cdot \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$
Results and Discussion
Monomer Synthesis

As shown in Scheme 1, the new bis(ether anhydride) was synthesized using a three-step synthetic procedure starting from the nucleophilic nitro-displacement reaction of $^ { 2 , 2 - }$bis(4-hydroxyphenyl) cyclododecane and 4-nitrophthalonitrile in dry DMF in the presence of potassium carbonate at room temperature. The nitro-displacement reaction was preferably carried out at low temperature (room temperature), than at higher temperature (over $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$since the products BCPPC were always dark in color when they were obtained at high temperature. The bis(ether dinitrile) BCPPC was then hydrolyzed in an alkaline solution in the presence of hydrogen peroxide to obtain the 1,1-bis[4- (3,4-dicarboxyphenoxy)phenyl]cyclododecane (BAPPC). It is worth noting that nitriles can be hydrolyzed to give either amides or carboxylic acids. Although the amide is being formed initially, carboxylic acid is the most common product since amides are hydrolyzed with acid or base. When carboxylic acid is desired, the reagent of choice is aqueous KOH containing about 6 to 12% hydrogen peroxide, although acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is also carried out frequently.<sup>[20]</sup> The bis(ether diacid) (BAPPC) was then cyclodehydrated to the bis(ether anhydride) BDPCD in the dehydrating agent such as a mixture of acetic anhydride and glacial acetic anhydride. The structure of these synthesized compounds was confirmed by elemental analysis, IR and NMR spectroscopy. The cyano group (C:N) of compound BCPPC was evident from the peak at 2 224 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$in the IR spectrum. However, in the IR spectrum of BCPPC, the cyano stretching vibration was absent, although a broad C(O)O–H absorption appeared in the region of 2 500–3 600 cm<sup>-1</sup>, and a C O stretching absorption appeared at 1 706 cm<sup>-1</sup>. The IR spectrum data of the bis(ether anhydride) BDPCD showed characteristic cyclic anhydride absorption at 1 840 and 1 $7 6 7 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$attributed to the asymmetrical and symmetrical stretching vibrations of C O of anhydride group, respectively. The corresponding $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra ofBHPC, BCPPC, BAPPC, and BDPCD are listed in the experimental section. These results clearly confirm that the dianhydride prepared herein is consistent with the proposed structure.
Preparation ofPoly(ether imide)s

The poly(ether imide)s were prepared by the conventional two-step polymerization method, as shown in Scheme 2, which involves ring-opening polyaddition of bis(ether anhydride) BDPCD with diamines DA-1 to DA-7 forming poly(ether amic acid) precursors PAA-1 to PAA-7 and subsequent chemical cyclodehydration. The poly(ether amic acid)s (PAA-1 to PAA-7) were prepared by gradually adding the bis(ether anhydride) BDPCD to the diamines (DA-1 to DA-7) in DMAc solution. The obtained viscous poly(ether amic acid) solution was then supplemented by dehydrating agents, such as a mixture of acetic anhydride and pyridine to yield poly(ether imide)s PI-1 to PI-7. The resulting poly(ether imide)s had inherent viscosities of 0.50–0.86 dL $\cdot \mathrm { { g } } ^ { - 1 }$(Table 2). The polymers exhibited ${ \vec { M } } _ { \mathrm { n } }$and $\overline { { M } } _ { \mathrm { w } }$in the range of16 000–63 000 and 32 000–115 000, respectively. The structure of the polymers was identified by IR and NMR spectroscopy. Specifically, the IR spectra of the poly(ether imide)s revealed that the characteristic bands around 1 768 and 1 $7 1 6 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$are commonly attributed to the asymmetric and symmetric stretches of carbonyl group of imides, respectively. The C–N band at $1 3 6 9 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$verified the formation of the imide structure. The NMR data of the polymer PI-1 are listed in the experimental section, and the resonance peaks at 168.0 and 167.9 ppm are ascribed to the carbon of the imide group. The elemental analysis data of these polyimides as listed in Table 1 are generally in good agreement with the respective structures for hydrogen, carbon, and nitrogen. All the polymer films could be obtained by the solution cast from their DMAc solution. All polymer films were transparent, tough and flexible. These films were subjected to both wide-angle X-ray and mechanical tests.

elements.text: Polymer Characterization

The solubility of these polyimides obtained by chemical imidization was tested in various solvents. The results are shown in Table 2. Polyimides PI-1 to PI-7 were most readily soluble in organic solvents exhibiting excellent solubility toward test solvents. At room temperature, they dissolved in a variety of solvents such as N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc), dimethylformamide (DMF), pyridine, cyclohexanone, and even in tetrahydrofuran. For comparison, polyimide Ref-1 containing biphenylene without pendant cyclododecylidene was further prepared from 4,4<sup>0</sup>-bis(4-aminophenoxy)biphenyl with dianhydride only containing the biphenylene group. It was observed that polyimide Ref-1 was nearly insoluble in the test solvents and showed poorer solubility than its analogous polymer PI-1. This may be due to the presence of the bulky pendant group which decreases the inter-chain interaction of rigid aromatic repeating units, resulting in enhanced solubility.<sup>[18]</sup> Upon comparison the solubility of poly(ether imide)s by introduction of cyclododecane group with the commercial poly(ether imide)s (ULTEM), it was observed that the poly(ether imide)s by introduction of cyclododecane group have shown better properties such as thermal properties, glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$(Table 3), and T (temperature at 10% weight loss). ULTEM has $T _ { \mathrm { g } } = 2 1 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$In addition, poly(ether imide)s by introduction of cyclododecane group could have good solubility in organic solvents such as NMP, DMAc, DMF, pyridine, cyclohexanone, and THF.

The crystallinity of the polyimides was estimated using X-ray diffractograms, indicating that all of the polymers presented amorphous patterns. This is reasonable because the bulky pendent cyclododecane group significantly increased the disorder in chains, and therefore caused less chain packing. The thermal properties of the poly(ether imide)s are tabulated in Table 3. Glass transition temperatures $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \ \mathrm { \gamma } } \mathrm { s } )$of these poly(ether imide)s, determined by means of differential scanning calorimeter (DSC), were in the range of $2 3 0 { - } 2 6 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$Upon comparison with the thermal properties, all the polyimides exhibited higher $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$values than the commercial available polyimide Ultem 1000 $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } = 2 1 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$. Especially, polymers PI-7 containing adamantane cardo groups revealed the highest $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$value compared with the other PIs without a cardo group. In general, the cardo group showed high $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$value due to the bulky pendent group, which inhibited the free rotation of the polymer backbone.<sup>[20,21]</sup> Incorporation of adamantane groups in the polymer backbone always leads to a significantly enhanced T<sub>g</sub> value.<sup>[22]</sup> $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$

elements.text: Thermogravimetric (TG) analysis revealed that these poly(ether imide)s showed good thermal stability. They were stable up to approximately $4 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$. The temperatures at 10% weight loss $( T _ { \mathrm { d 1 0 } } )$reached to $4 3 4 - 4 6 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$and 407– $4 5 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$in nitrogen and in air atmosphere, respectively. Upon comparison the thermal properties of herein with the alicyclic poly(ether imide)s reported in our previous study, it was observed that the poly(ether imide) (PI-3) by introduction of cyclododecane group has higher $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$value than Ref-2 and Ref-3 containing $\mathrm { k i n k } ^ { [ 6 ] }$and tert-butylcyclohexane alicyclic<sup>[23]</sup> groups, respectively. It means that the introduction of cyclododecane group into the polymer backbone could enhance the thermal property effectively.

The films had tensile strength of 80–102 MPa, elongation at break of $6 - 1 0 \%$and initial modulus of 1.7–2.0 GPa. Most of the films were strong and tough. The data of pretilt angle of polyimides (PI-1 to PI-7) have been provided in Table 3. These polyimides have per tilt angle of0.21–2.30. It was observed that polymer PI-7 containing rigid adamantane pendent group exhibited the highest pretilt angle (y) value $( \theta = 2 . 3 0 ^ { \circ } )$.
Conclusions

A new bis(ether anhydride) bearing both flexible ether and pendent cyclododecylidene units between the phenylene units, was successfully prepared in three steps starting from 2,2-bis(4-hydroxyphenyl) cyclododecane. A series of poly(ether imide)s with moderate to high molecular weights were obtained from this dianhydride monomer and various diamines. The polymers with cyclododecane group had good thermal properties such as glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$and $T _ { \mathrm { d } 1 0 }$(temperature at 10% weight loss). These poly(ether imide)s showed excellent solubility in various organic solvents. Thus, these new highly soluble poly(ether imide)s could be considered as novel processable high-performance polymeric materials.
